clue.text: Never miss quiz show which inspired four groups of four in this grid

definitions.meaning: first meaning: if every shot you take hits

definitions.text: quiz show which inspired four groups of four in this grid
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the BBC quiz whose wall round asks players to sort sixteen clues into four linked groups

explanation.walkthrough: The grid holds four themed sets of four: NATO alphabet words, months, Dahl's chocolate factory children and old men or emperors, as in the quiz's connecting wall.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is both an instruction never to fail to hit and the title of the BBC quiz show built on finding links.

clue.text: Prestigious award presented by no-mark?

parts.note: O looks like a zero, nothing
a scar is a mark left on the skin

explanation.surface: A sneer that a coveted prize has been handed out by some worthless nobody.
explanation.walkthrough: A no-mark is British slang for a nobody; split it into 'no' and 'mark'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Oscar is the Academy Award, the best-known film prize in Hollywood.

clue.text: Shakespearean king determined Christmas must be overturned

indicators.note: something overturned is turned upside down, so in a down entry the joined words read from the bottom up

parts.note: set on something means determined to do it
Noel is another word for Christmas

explanation.surface: A royal resolving that Christmas be cancelled, like a Puritan monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Leontes is the jealous king of Sicilia in The Winter's Tale.

clue.text: See 1
Maybe Methuselah cracked almond

indicators.note: a cracked nut is broken apart, so the letters fall into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The setter, who signs himself Methuselah, has gone nuts.
explanation.walkthrough: Methuselah is also this puzzle's setter, so the surface reads as a joke at his own expense.
explanation.definitionFit: Methuselah, said to have lived 969 years, is the Bible's oldest man, an example of an elderly male.

clue.text: Happening around the fifth, something burning this month

indicators.note: turning around faces the other way, so the word for happening runs backwards

parts.note: an event that is on is happening
V is the Roman numeral five
an ember is a glowing piece of coal or wood

explanation.surface: Bonfire Night on the fifth, with something smouldering, falls in the month of the puzzle's publication.
explanation.walkthrough: Guy Fawkes Night, Britain's bonfire and fireworks night, is on the fifth of this month.
explanation.definitionFit: The puzzle appeared in the eleventh month, so the current month is the one named here.

clue.text: King casually calls for toast with pork pie

definitions.note: the familiar form of a king's name, Charles

parts.note: to char is to scorch, as you would toast bread
Cockney rhyming slang: pork pie means lie
joins the two pieces

explanation.surface: A monarch informally orders toast to go with a pork pie, a British cold meat pastry.
explanation.walkthrough: Pork pie for lie is Cockney rhyming slang, often shortened to porky.
explanation.definitionFit: A king named Charles would be called this nickname in casual speech.

clue.text: Legendary hunter mounting leopard or minotaur hides

indicators.note: in a down clue, mounting means climbing upwards, so the letters read bottom to top
the words conceal the letters inside them, running across the gap between

parts.note: the letters straddle the end of the first animal, the 'or' and the start of the bull-man

explanation.surface: A mythic huntsman climbing onto the pelts of the big cats and monsters he has killed.
explanation.definitionFit: Nimrod is the mighty hunter before the Lord in Genesis.

clue.text: Leading lady disseminating OC trivia

indicators.note: disseminating scatters things widely, so these letters are spread into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A film star spreading gossip about the Officer Commanding.
explanation.definitionFit: Queen Victoria led the nation, so she was a leading lady in the literal sense.

clue.text: Lump of something turning young horse's stomach

indicators.note: turning round makes a part of the word face the other way
the stomach sits in the middle of the body, so only the central letters are turned

parts.note: a colt is a young male horse

explanation.surface: Something that upsets a foal's digestion.
explanation.walkthrough: The stomach is the middle of the word, so only its two central letters swap.
explanation.definitionFit: A clot is a thickened mass, such as of blood or cream, a lump formed from some substance.

clue.text: Avoid the missing vowels round? Great resolution!

indicators.note: the Only Connect round named this strips every A, E, I, O and U from the words
in that quiz round the remaining letters are re-spaced and must be sorted, so they come in a new order

parts.note: the two words with their vowels removed

explanation.surface: A quiz contestant hoping to skip the dreaded Missing Vowels round, then cheering a fine decision.
explanation.walkthrough: Missing Vowels is the last round of Only Connect, the theme quiz.
explanation.definitionFit: High-definition television gives a sharp picture, that is a great screen resolution.

clue.text: Excuse getting both Caliban and Cain out of prison

indicators.note: taking something out of a word removes those letters, here from each of both names

parts.note: taken as written; both says the next name loses the same letters
taken as written
the can is slang for prison

explanation.surface: Two literary villains, Shakespeare's monster and the Bible's first murderer, both have a reason to walk free.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the letters of CAN from each name: CALIBAN leaves ALIB and CAIN leaves I.
explanation.definitionFit: An alibi is a claim of being elsewhere, the classic excuse offered against a charge.

clue.text: Top spy replaces lead for fancy audio equipment

indicators.note: the first letter, the lead, is swapped out and the spy's letter goes in its place

parts.note: M is the head of the secret service in the Bond stories
to fancy something is to like it

explanation.surface: A senior agent swapping his lead for some smart recording gear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' looks like a cable for the audio kit; it means the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A mike is a microphone, the basic piece of sound recording gear.

clue.text: Something in your eye when drinking last of precious wine

indicators.note: something drinking takes a liquid into itself, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: the retina is the light-sensitive layer in the eye

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter only

parts.note: final letter

explanation.surface: A drinker noticing something in the eye while sipping the dregs of a valued vintage.
explanation.definitionFit: Retsina is a Greek white wine flavoured with pine resin.

clue.text: Two informants — one going underground

parts.note: a mole is a spy planted inside an organisation
a rat is someone who tells on others

explanation.surface: A pair of informers, one of whom vanishes into hiding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going underground' sounds like a spy fleeing; it is a burrowing animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The mole rat is an African rodent that lives in burrows below the surface.

clue.text: Several points covered in oddly airy response

indicators.note: something covered in another thing sits inside it
oddly means taking the letters in odd positions, first, third and so on

parts.note: first and third letters
four compass points: north, south, west, east

explanation.surface: Several matters handled in a strangely breezy reply.
explanation.definitionFit: An answer is a reply or response to a question.

clue.text: One who founded dynasty in America after gold rush

indicators.note: after says the American piece follows the earlier ones in the answer

parts.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold
a gust is a sudden rush of wind
US is short for the United States

explanation.surface: A man who founded a family empire in the US during the gold rush.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the 1849 Californian gold rush; the pieces are a symbol and a gust.
explanation.definitionFit: Augustus was the first Roman emperor, founder of the Julio-Claudian dynasty.

clue.text: Footballer put off outside goal

indicators.note: one piece stands outside the other, wrapping round it

parts.note: to defer is to postpone
an end is an aim or goal

explanation.surface: A player kept out of position, standing beyond the goal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goal' looks like football; it means an aim.
explanation.definitionFit: A defender is a footballer whose job is to stop the other side scoring.

clue.text: After bungling order, he'd be on a plank

indicators.note: once the order is bungled, the letters stand in a muddled new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A pirate who botched an order would be made to walk the plank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plank' seems to be the pirate's board; it is British slang for a dim person.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are informal insults for a stupid person.

clue.text: Politician's lying finally finished — and also not

indicators.note: finally points to the very end of the word, its closing letter

parts.note: final letter
something over is finished
nor means and also not

explanation.surface: A politician's lies are at last over, or maybe not.
explanation.definitionFit: A US state governor is an elected politician heading a state government.

clue.text: No end of nutrition for wild flower

indicators.note: no says that letter is absent, taken away

parts.note: wild in the sense of fierce

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter

parts.note: final letter

explanation.surface: A hedgerow bloom that needs plenty of feeding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild flower' looks like one phrase; wild is the wordplay and flower alone the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The violet is a small purple-flowered plant.

clue.text: Socialist policy which may be a deal breaker

parts.note: red is the colour of socialism
a party line is its policy

explanation.surface: A left-wing policy that could wreck a negotiation.
explanation.definitionFit: A red line is a limit that cannot be crossed in talks, the point at which a deal fails.

clue.text: Dahl character — a Salt knocked back after seeing some geese?

parts.note: flying geese form a V

indicators.note: knocking something back sends it the opposite way, so this part reads backwards

parts.note: taken as written
to salt meat is to cure it

explanation.surface: The spoilt girl from Charlie and the Chocolate Factory being thrown out, after demanding the golden goose.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue names her surname, Salt, which is wordplay; she is thrown down a rubbish chute after the golden-egg geese.
explanation.definitionFit: Veruca Salt is a spoilt child in Roald Dahl's Charlie and the Chocolate Factory.

clue.text: I could go on horse to make an impression

parts.note: et cetera, and so on, said when a list could continue
horse is slang for heroin, abbreviated H

explanation.surface: Someone boasting they could ride on to leave their mark.
explanation.definitionFit: To etch is to cut a design into a surface, making an impression in it.

clue.text: A slap-up spread somewhere in Scandinavia

indicators.note: a spread is laid out across the table, these letters set out in a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A lavish feast laid on in a Nordic town.
explanation.walkthrough: A slap-up meal is British for a lavish one.
explanation.definitionFit: Uppsala is a Swedish university city, one place in the Scandinavian region.

clue.text: Clergyman's a bit of a booby, possibly dropping a tablet

indicators.note: dropping something lets it fall away, so that letter is lost

parts.words: a bit of a booby, possibly
parts.note: the booby is a seabird, and a plume is one piece of its plumage
E is slang for an ecstasy pill

explanation.surface: A priest's a bit of an idiot, perhaps letting a pill fall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Booby' suggests a fool or a breast; it is a seabird.
explanation.definitionFit: Father is the title of a Catholic priest.

clue.text: Foot spy dipped into water? On the contrary

indicators.note: one thing dipped into another goes inside it
this flips the roles just described, so the water goes inside the spy instead

parts.note: to spy is to see
a pond is a body of water

explanation.surface: Someone dipping a toe into water.
explanation.walkthrough: Taken literally the spy goes into the water; 'On the contrary' flips it so the water goes inside the spy.
explanation.definitionFit: A spondee is a metrical foot of two stressed syllables.

clue.text: Unprofessional cop openly pockets a little drink

indicators.note: pockets means holds tucked away, so the run of letters lies inside the words

parts.note: the letters run from the tail of the first word to the start of the third

explanation.surface: A bent police officer openly takes a small drink.
explanation.definitionFit: An alcopop is a sweet fizzy alcoholic drink sold in small bottles.

clue.text: Frolic on adult beach in Spain

parts.note: to frolic is to play
A is a film certificate for adult; 'on' puts it after

explanation.surface: Grown-up fun on a Spanish beach.
explanation.definitionFit: Playa is the Spanish word for beach.

clue.text: Organs of state heartlessly start on immigrants

indicators.note: with its heart gone, one of the middle letters is removed

parts.note: to utter is to state

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter

explanation.surface: Government bodies callously begin on immigrants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organs of state' looks like one phrase for institutions; 'state' belongs to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Uteri is the plural of uterus, the womb, so they are organs.

clue.text: One bouncing off the walls ultimately became lethargic couch potato

indicators.note: ultimately means at the very end, so each word gives its last letter

parts.note: the final letter of each of the four words

explanation.surface: A hyperactive person who eventually turned into a sluggish couch potato.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bouncing off the walls' suggests hyperactivity; it is literal, for sound.
explanation.definitionFit: An echo is a sound reflected back from a surface.

clue.text: Get shot of initially agreeable relative

parts.note: to pap is to photograph like the paparazzi

indicators.note: initially means at the beginning, so only the opening letter counts

parts.note: first letter

explanation.surface: Getting rid of a relative who was pleasant at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get shot of' is British for get rid of; here it means take a photo of.
explanation.definitionFit: Papa is an old-fashioned word for father, a family relative.

clue.text: Students of French enthralled by derrières

indicators.note: enthralled means held captive, so one piece is held inside the other

parts.note: derrières are backsides
de is French for of

explanation.surface: Learners of French captivated by bottoms.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a reader is a senior university lecturer, but more generally someone who studies texts.
explanation.definitionFit: Readers are people who study books, so students of a text.

clue.text: Pop art?

parts.note: surface reading: the 1960s movement of Warhol and Lichtenstein
setter's reading: an art movement whose name is baby talk for a father, Pop

explanation.walkthrough: Pop is a father; the art movement's name is a child's word for one.
explanation.definitionFit: Dada was an early twentieth-century anti-art movement, and dada is infant talk for daddy.
